TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
THURSDAY, 2 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 9:35 AM (AEST)
DAY 30
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MR MIN GUO, for Ms Rachelle Miller
MR PHILIP SOLOMON KC, for The Hon Alan Tudge MP
MR PAUL JEFFREYS, for The Hon Alan Tudge MP
MR ARTHUR MOSES SC, for The Hon Christian Porter
MR GABRIEL PERRY, for The Hon Christian Porter

COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery. We have got Mr Tudge back. The appearances are the
same. You now have a junior, do you, Mr Solomon?
MR SOLOMON: Notwithstanding my assistance that I needed to turn the microphone on, I
failed to.
COMMISSIONER: That's what the junior is for.
MR SOLOMON: You can rest assured I will let him know. With Mr Jeffreys, I appear this
morning.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Mr Moses, you are here for Mr Porter, I think?
MS MOSES: If it pleases the Commission, I appear with my learned friend Mr Perry for
Mr Porter. If it please the Commission.
COMMISSIONER: And all as usual for you, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: It is as usual, thank you, Commissioner.
MR GREGGERY: Commissioner, my apologies for the slight delay. That was my fault this
morning. Mr Tudge, to conclude the topic yesterday, I take it you gave no standing
direction to the Department to investigate matters where there was a suggestion of a
suicide associated with the receipt of letters under the Scheme?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: No.
MR GREGGERY: You would appreciate, of course, that a standing direction like that had
the advantage of identifying potential systemic issues as opposed to issues which might be
discrete or personal to the recipient?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Repeat that question again?
MR GREGGERY: A standing direction like that would ensure that investigations had the
capacity to identify systemic issues in matters where there was a suggestion of a suicide
associated with the receipt of letters, in addition to the matters personal to the recipient,
which might be relevant consideration.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Potentially.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Potentially.
MR GREGGERY: Having had overnight to think about it, can you now recall any reason why
you would not have asked for an investigation in the matter we discussed late yesterday?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: In relation to this particular matter, I don't recall what information
was provided to me. There's no evidence in all of the documents that I've looked at, which

Chief of Staff. I can't recall that verbal Briefing and what he said, and therefore what my
response was. I do know that I've made - I requested two investigations for suicides in the
past, one of which we discussed yesterday, and there was one - I believe previous to
that - [redacted], from memory.
In both of those cases, my recollection is that they did involve debt notices being received
and the allegation that that caused distress to the individual. In this case, again, just
reiterate I don't know what I was told verbally, but from the written information that was
presented, at least to Mr Asten upon which he was relying upon in the absence of other
information, it indicated that it wasn't connected to a debt notice as such. And that may
have been the reason, but I'm speculating there.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. As a general proposition, was it the case that the suggestion that a
suicide might be related to the Scheme generally was insufficient to compel an
investigation into the circumstances?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Again, I'm speculating because I - I can't recall the conversation
which I assumed I had with Mr Asten, my Chief of Staff at the time. It was a verbal
communication. I don't believe that I was - had any communication with the Department
in relation to it, which typically I would assume that I - that I would, in fact, would get a
verbal - would get a written Briefing in relation to it.
MR GREGGERY: Certainly you could have obtained whatever information you wanted from
the Department at your request?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I could have done. And, again, I don't know what information I
was provided to - provided with by my Chief of Staff at the time.
MR GREGGERY: The evidence you gave yesterday about the annual report, the reference
to approximately 5000 threats of suicide as part of the reason why this matter might not
be significant to your recollection, does that suggest that, ultimately, the question of
whether suicides were associated with the Scheme or not was an insufficient reason to
stop the continuation of the savings measure?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Just repeat that question again to me, if you could?
MR GREGGERY: The question of whether suicides were associated with the Scheme was an
insufficient reason, I take it, to put a pause on the measure, that is, the savings measure,
review whether, in fact, it was causally related to suicides.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Any suggestion that there was distress caused by the Scheme
appeared, to me, to be connected with the implementation problems of the OCI, which I
was very, very focused on addressing. Had a laser-like focus on addressing those
problems. And ensuring all of the issues which we went through yesterday, and more
which we didn't touch on, and including the fact that a Compliance Officer would be
placed back into the role to check before any debt issues were raised. So my belief at that
time - and I - my belief at that time was that that was the cause for the distress and that
those were the issues, which I felt as if we had addressed reasonably well.

MR GREGGERY: And did you then assume that any suggestion of suicide associated with
the Scheme thereafter was not a sufficient reason to conduct a further review of the
Scheme generally or the particular circumstances?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I don't recall any other suicide being brought to my attention
where there was even a suggestion that it was at all - there was a suggestion at all that
there was a connection to any welfare compliance measure. Other than the one that you
have brought to my attention and that I've indicated would have received, I presume, a
verbal Briefing from my Chief of Staff.
MR GREGGERY: But one would be enough, wouldn't it? It's a Budget savings measure,
Mr Tudge. One suggestion of suicide associated with the Scheme would be enough.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: And I appreciate the way you're connecting the Budget savings as
the issue in your questions. As I gave evidence yesterday, Budget savings were a
component and overall welfare integrity was an important element of it as well. Any
suicide is tragic. We don't - we never know what ultimately causes someone to take their
life. Sadly, it occurs too often in Australia, and it's been a big focus - was a big focus of our
Government.
COMMISSIONER: You didn't hear the name Cath Madgwick or anything about her?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I recall that name, Cath Madgwick. I don't- I can't recall the details
of that, but I do recall that name.
COMMISSIONER: That didn't spark any anxiety or make you think there might be an issue
to be reviewed?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: You would have to remind me of the details of that case, because I
can't -
COMMISSIONER: It was a mother who had lost her son and it's not entirely clear that it
was Robodebt, but it was possible that it was. It doesn't ring any bells?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: What period of time was that?
COMMISSIONER: I don't know. Can you assist with that at all?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It - I don't -
MR GREGGERY: I think it might have been after the Minister -
COMMISSIONER: After Mr Tudge.
MR GREGGERY: 2019, I think. It will be a question for subsequent Ministers, I expect. But
in any event, Mr Tudge, you would have been informed, rather than speculating about
potential causes, if an investigation had been directed to be undertaken by the
Department?

what he said to me. The information available which was presented to him indicated that
the connection was the receipt of a discrepancy letter, not the receipt of a debt notice.
And at that stage, Mr Greggery, certainly we had gone to great efforts to ensure the clarity
of those discrepancy letters and to ensure that it very clearly stated in those discrepancy
letters that this is not a debt letter.
And I don't have a copy in front of me, but my strong recollection was that I wanted
precisely to ensure that those letters were clearly stated that this is not a debt letter,
there may be an explanation for the discrepancy, and there's a 1800 contact number if
you would like to speak to someone about it. And that was the information which at least
appeared in the evidence we saw yesterday to Mr Asten, and upon which, in the absence
of other information provided to Mr Asten, would have been the only basis upon which he
could verbally brief me. And I can't recall -
MR GREGGERY: You are speculating there. You don't know what contact he had with the
Department beyond that email?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Well, I did ask yesterday, because it says in the email that he
wanted a further Briefing by the end of day, and you suggested to me yesterday,
Mr Greggery, that there was no further documentation, at least, available following up
from that request.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, but you don't know what contact he had with the Department apart
from an email.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: No, I don't. No, I don't. That's true.
MR GREGGERY: One distinction between the circumstances Mr Cauzzo's suicide, in which
you did order an investigation of the Department, and this particular matter, where you
did not, is that Mr Cauzzo's matter had hit the media. Was that significant?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I don't believe that the [redacted] matter - the [redacted] case had
hit the media. I can't recall that.
MR GREGGERY: Well, if you can't recall something, it plainly can't answer my question, can
it?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: No, but it's important in terms of - because your suggestion in the
question is that I only did this because it hit the media, and in the case of [redacted] where
I did, I think it was the first time when I had requested a formal investigation. I don't think
it had hit the media. My recollection is that I was encouraged to do so in that instance by
Jenny Macklin, who had an interest, I think, knew the family and - was a constituent of
hers when she was a Member of Parliament, and I had a lot of respect for Jenny Macklin
and took that on board.
MR GREGGERY: That suggests that it was a consideration external to the circumstances in
which it occurred which propelled that investigation.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: My point is -

MR GREGGERY: Equivalent to something being in the media. More circumstances external
to the point.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You responded when there was an issue to be dealt with beyond the
particular circumstances of the suicide.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I suppose the point I was trying to get at, it was that the
implication of your question was that I only did it because of the media.
MR GREGGERY: That is the direct question I'm putting to you.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes, and I'm suggesting that the evidence would show that I, in
fact, did investigations in the absence of media as well, which would prove to be contrary
to the point that you're putting to me.
MR GREGGERY: Well, you appreciated in the circumstance where Ms Macklin raised an
issue with you, if you didn't do an investigation, it was likely to hit the media.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: No, no. In fact, I recall having a discussion with Ms Macklin about
it, that she didn't want to make an issue out of it. She was genuinely trying to get to the
bottom of it. And, as I said, I had a good relationship with Ms Macklin. I worked with her
previously even before being a Member of Parliament. And we went about that
investigation.
MR GREGGERY: Again, you accept it was an external prompt which caused you to take an
investigative role in that circumstance.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Well, in that instance, I do accept that it was a prompt by
Ms Macklin. That's my recollection and I think it's an accurate recollection.
MR GREGGERY: Did you have to be asked to do an investigation or did it have to be in the
media?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It depends on the circumstances, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: How do you identify those circumstances where you, in fact, conduct an
investigation?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: The investigation of Mr Cauzzo, if that's pronouncing his name
correctly, was done by the Department. A separate group - a separate group of people,
though, to people who did the Compliance Officers. It appears - I will just leave it there.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. At paragraph 88 of your Statement, you say:
The broad rollout of the OCI began in late September of 2016, with larger numbers of
letters being sent to recipients starting in early October.

of the document which you footnote behind tab 82 in the bundle. It is Exhibit 2010. If you
turn to tab 82 and if 2010 could be displayed on the screen. The date of your signature is 6
March 2016
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And - which I think is incorrect.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I think that's incorrect. I think it should be 6 March 2017.
MR GREGGERY: 2017. Thank you. Because it is Ministerial Brief 17-000172. You can see
that in paragraph 1 of the key points, your chief of staff requested an overview of the
government decision points in the lead-up to the commencement of OCI and a list and
summary of Briefs and documents is at Attachment A.
Paragraph 3 refers to a Briefing, the former Minister for Human Services, The Hon Marise
Payne MP, in which options were outlined to improve compliance to the former services
Minister, Minister Morrison. And then the former Minister agreed to pursue employment
income data-matching initiative and the summary of the 2015/16 Budget - Social Services
Portfolio Budget Submission is at Attachment B.
Now, on the document that you have - and we might just briefly bring it up on the
screen - you can see if we go to Attachment B, page 0065, it is completely redacted. This is
introducing why I'm about to tender a new document. And if you - but if before we come
to that you go to the page ending 0060, which is Attachment A, and you can see B15/125
at the bottom of the page there, and there is a summary of it. It is the Brief referred to in
paragraph 3 of the introduction. It carries over to the next page.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Mmm.
MR GREGGERY: I'm testing the document management staff at the moment. But you can
see there the summary identifies the Brief to Minister Morrison which outlined a number
of options, including new data sources for automated data matching, increased use of
Employment Income Matching by the introduction of a new approach to reconciling
information declared to the Department by the customer with information from the ATO
by their online account using PAYG information from the ATO from 2010 to 2013. And the
last sentence, says:
Legislative change was identified in the Brief and DSS were working on developing this
proposal.
You can see that?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And I take it because this was a Brief from your predecessor, it was
available to you in the records held by the Minister's Office.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I don't know the answer to that question. And depends on

MR GREGGERY: It wasn't. I take it you didn't go looking for it?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I don't know if a Minister has access to former Ministers' Briefing
materials. That's not something that I would immediately spring to mind even now, and
I've held, I think, four or so different portfolios.
MR GREGGERY: You could have asked the Department for a copy?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Again, I don't know whether it was in my mind that I had access to
briefing materials to former Ministers.
MR GREGGERY: My question is that you could have asked the Department.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Of course, I could have asked, "Can I please have access to that
briefing material following" -
MR GREGGERY: Because as at 6 March 2016 after your Chief of Staff requested an
overview of government decision points, there was a flag here that legislative change was
a consideration in respect of the origins of the OCI Scheme.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Right. Sorry, you are still referring to Attachment A at the top
there?
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: If Exhibit 2669 could be brought up. This is the Briefing in full, Mr Tudge.
Had you asked for a copy of it or found out whether you could have access to a copy of it,
it would have been provided with this document, the source document for the summary
provided to your Chief of Staff, which provided more than the summary of the question
about legislative change but identified the full context in which it was -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Do I have that in my bundle?
MR GREGGERY: No, you don't. If we can turn to - I think it's page 7 of 10, from
recollection.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: So that is a Cabinet document? I would not have been able to
access a Cabinet document.
MR GREGGERY: No, it's not a Cabinet document.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It says "Cabinet" at the bottom.
MR GREGGERY: It might say that, but it's not. I mean, the one we were just looking at says
"protected sensitive Cabinet", which gave you the summary of these things and it wasn't a
Cabinet document, was it, Mr Tudge?

between was it a document which goes to the Cabinet for presentation to the Cabinet, no,
it is not such a document. Is it a Cabinet-protected document because it goes to the
formulation of Cabinet materials, then, yes, it appears to me, looking at it here, that it is a
Cabinet-protected document. That is the classification of that document, and when I said
this would be a Cabinet document, I was referring to the classification, as opposed to a
document which would appear for all of the Cabinet Ministers for their consideration.
MR GREGGERY: Right.
COMMISSIONER: It was a fair way back from that. It just agreed that the Departments
would work on New Policy Proposals
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I am only referring to the classification given.
COMMISSIONER: Alright.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: And I don't believe I would have had access to a document which
was classified as Cabinet if I was a non-Cabinet Minister.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry, it was page 10 of 17.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: In a previous Cabinet that I was not connected to. That's all I'm
saying, Commissioner.
MR GREGGERY: This is the proposal referred to in the summary sought by your Chief of
Staff about the key decision points.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Is it possible to get a hard copy of this, Mr Greggery? Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: It is the page which is summarised as:
Increased use of Employment Income Matching by the introduction of a new approach to
reconciling information declared by to the Department by the customer with information
from the ATO.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You can see that the third dot point and the fourth dot point indicate the
changes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Which were identified in the proposal. You can see that?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I can see that. Sorry -
MR GREGGERY: It's also identified in the first dot point, that it was a new approach to
reconciling information.

MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes, I can see that.
MR GREGGERY: Just on the factual summary there that's highlighted in passages called
out, can you identify any meaningful difference between the proposal as it's described
there and what you came to understand in January 2017 of the OCI process?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: From both of those bullet points that you are referring to?
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: If I may just take my time to read them again?
MR GREGGERY: Of course.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: So just, sorry, go back to the precise question, Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: On the factual summary in the highlighted passages, can you identify any
meaningful difference between the proposal as it's described there and what you came to
understand in January 2017 of the OCI process?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I can.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: This is early stage of a proposal, by the looks of it, before any New
Policy Proposals are developed.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, I'm interested in the difference.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: But the difference is as you put to me yesterday, which is in the
first two lines of the first bullet point:
The customer will be presented via their online account with the information obtained
from the ATO.
Now, I don't believe that was the case, as we discussed yesterday.
MR GREGGERY: Because it was contained in a letter under OCI?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Sorry?
MR GREGGERY: How is that different, you say, to the OCI process?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: From memory - and I'm going back to thinking about the initial
screens of the OCI - I don't know if it did contain the - you put to me yesterday was there a
comparison between what was self-declared versus what the ATO says on an average
basis, and I - which is the implication from these first two sentences, and I don't believe

MR GREGGERY: Sorry, if I understand your answer correctly, what you are saying is that,
under OCI, the customer was provided with information obtained from the ATO but not
the amount that they declared to Centrelink.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I'm just trying to - I'm just trying to recall exactly what those
screens did contain.
MR GREGGERY: You gave evidence yesterday, Mr Tudge, that the discrepancy letter, the
first in the process, identified ATO information but it didn't identify the information that
the person declared to Centrelink.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: That's right, in the letter, and here is referring to their online
account, so I'm -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I'm putting my mind to what that online account said rather than
what the letter said, because it's precisely referring to the online account. And I don't
think, as you were alluding to yesterday, that in that online account it had the rows of
numbers lined up against each other.
MR GREGGERY: That is, it didn't contain the information the person declared to
Centrelink?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I don't - I can't recall, but I don't believe so. It certainly didn't do as
you described, and that's what I'm trying to highlight in those first two sentences.
MR GREGGERY: Was there any other distinction that you can identify of -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Or that first sentence, I should say. I don't believe so, but you may
be able to prompt me.
MR GREGGERY: I'm suggesting it's, in substance, the same as the OCI process.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Well, in substance, the two bullet points are, and I had to read
very closely and recollect our conversation yesterday to point out the difference precisely
with that first sentence.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Mr Tudge.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: So I'm trying to be very precise.
MR GREGGERY: If you could go to the last dot point on the page. This is where the
reference to legislative change in the summary that you were provided comes from.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Mmm.
MR GREGGERY: If you could read that closely as well.

MR GREGGERY: Subject to your concern that you might not have had access to this
document even if you asked for it because of its classification -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: And a different portfolio.
MR GREGGERY: Just - it's your portfolio, isn't it? The Department of Human Services
Executive Minute signed by the Minister for Human Services? I'm sorry.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Sorry, this one is signed by the Minister for Social Services.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry I'm looking at the wrong document. Yes, to the Minister for Human
Services for information.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It is copied to the Minister for Human Services for information.
MR GREGGERY: That's right, yes. Subject to the qualification about the classification and
the additional qualification, you say, that it was merely copied to your predecessor, you
had within your means of knowledge, as at 6 March 2017, the ability to know that DSS had
at some point advised legislative change was required for what became the OCI program?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: They are very big assumptions, and I didn't seek -
MR GREGGERY: I included them in the question. Is the answer then yes?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It's subject to me being able to access it. Sorry, going back to - can
I have a look at the previous document? Because you are referring to the previous
document which I was referred to, made a reference to this document.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: And the previous document -
MR GREGGERY: Mr Tudge, my question doesn't have anything to do with the previous
document. My question has to do with your ability to access this document. Subject to be
being able to -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: But I didn't access to this document, is why I was wanting to refer
back to the previous document.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, that doesn't answer my question. Please listen to my question,
Mr Tudge. Subject to your ability to access the document because of its classification or
because it was copied to your predecessor -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: - two caveats you have identified, it was otherwise within your means of
knowledge, had you got the document, that DSS had advised legislative change would be
needed to implement what became the OCI system.

MR GREGGERY: You could have got the document, read that.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: It is - subject to those, I would have got the document, read it very
closely and picked that one up, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And given, as you say, your laser-like focus in January 2017 on the
system and that this was a Brief signed to you 17 February 2017 which drew your
attention to the history of decision-making, one would think your laser-like focus extended
to this document as well?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: I might give a couple of responses to that question, if I may.
MR GREGGERY: Absolutely.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: One being that my laser-like focus was very much on the matters
which were within my authority, which was the implementation issues which we've
discussed. The second point, though, is that even if I looked at this document -
MR GREGGERY: You are referring to the February 2015 Executive Minute?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: The Executive Minute, yes. Even if I - even if I was able to access
this document, did access this document, read this document closely, saw the bullet
points on the bottom of page - the bottom of page 10 of a 17-page document, I would
have noted, Mr Greggery, that - if I was reading it that closely, I would have also noted
that this was very early on in the development of these proposals. So it was
recommending here - and I'm examining this - that it's agreed to the development of the
package of New Policy Proposals with the concepts outlined here to give an indication to
the Minister for Social Services that this is broadly what we are thinking.
The next step of the development, of course, is the development of a New Policy Proposal,
and in that New Policy Proposal process is where the full legal lens gets put over it,
including in - having done many - a checklist which says - I can't remember the precise
words, but it might even say, "Is legislation required" and there's a checklist which says
either yes or no. And that is contained in the documents which then go to the Cabinet.
Before they even get into the Cabinet room, not only does that checklist have to be ticked,
ie, that the Department of Social Services would have had to assure themselves of the
legality of it to make that tick, but then the Attorney-General's Department also is able to
provide comment and does provide comment, typically always from a legal perspective on
the proposals.
They don't - and they are highlighted for the Cabinet if a proposal requires legislation.
Because it's an important thing for the Cabinet to know, as to whether or not this requires
legislation, because it changes the dynamic of a - of a proposal, particularly if you've got a
difficult Senate. So my point -
MR GREGGERY: You're speaking from your knowledge now or from your knowledge of
Cabinet process back then? Because you didn't hold a Cabinet position back then.

MR GREGGERY: Okay.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Which you are, in any case, even as a Parliamentary Secretary,
which I was in the previous - I was for three years before becoming a Minister. But I
certainly understand that today, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. Again, I'm dealing with your knowledge at the time.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes. But I can't distinguish, and I apologise that I can't distinguish
my knowledge at the time of the Cabinet process in detail compared to what I obviously
do know today.
MR GREGGERY: I understand. One of the central points you made in your response was
that even if you had have read this closely, you would have appreciated that something
appeared, on your assumption, to change between this point and its approval as a Budget
Measure.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Absolutely. That it doesn't go - I shouldn't elaborate. I should just
stop.
MR GREGGERY: That's alright. The - if we return, then, to document 2010, this is the
document signed by you 6 March 2017, which contains the summary of the decision
points in the lead-up to the commencement of OCI.
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Paragraph 3, as I read out, in the last sentence says that the summary of
the 2015-16 Budget, Social Services Portfolio Budget Submission is Attachment B. And that
was the document which was on the screen which was fully redacted. And, to be clear, a
Portfolio Budget Submission is a document that went before Cabinet, to your
understanding?
Commissioner: Mr Tudge?
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Yes, sorry, I'm just reading this closely before I answer, if I may.
COMMISSIONER: I thought it was a more general question about -
THE HON ALAN TUDGE: Sorry, the more general question.
COMMISSIONER: - whether a Portfolio Budget Submission would go to Cabinet.
